title: Finally Saw Heaven’s Gate  and I have a question

commenti.body:
Where did you see it? A lot of services have something quite close to the director’s cut, although the Criterion cut is the ‘director approved’ version. 

I mean, for me, as a fan, the rollerskate dance is a top 10 scene in all of cinema. If that didn’t get ya - and not arguing taste - I don’t think the director’s cut will change your mind. It’s the same film, everything you said is true.

I saw it on Amazon prime.   

Yeah I kind of figured it wasn’t for me but never hurts to ask

Oh yeah, for sure. Director's Cuts can make all the diff. The theatrical cut was sheared to bits - I think they took an hour out. But the Prime cut, where I first saw it, is pretty similar to the final Director's Cut.
Are you in the 'misunderstood masterpiece' camp when it comes to this film?

Not exactly? My favorite films are the overly ambitious ones - they could be amazing, like 2001 or Lawrence of Arabia. They could be terrible, like CATS and Exorcist II - The Heretic.

I like films that are just impossibly grand in inventing a world. For example, they build a \*whole ass\* replication of downtown Helena, MT from the turn of the century for Heaven's Gate, and it's only in a couple shots. The roller-skate hootenanny is so marvelous. 

I think Heaven's Gate's problems, and they are definitely there, are way outweighed by the grandiosity of its vision. We'll likely never see an American film production on such a grand scale again. Even Marty's Killers of the Flower Moon had to rely on CGI for some sets and extras.

>I like films that are just impossibly grand in inventing a world. For example, they build a \*whole ass\* replication of downtown Helena, MT from the turn of the century for Heaven's Gate, and it's only in a couple shots. The roller-skate hootenanny is so marvelous.

I very much agree with this, but also think that *McCabe & Mrs. Miller* beat *Heaven's Gate* at this game nine years earlier. In the words of [Chelsea Wessels](https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-film-preservation-board/documents/mccabe.pdf), 

>Moving all the crew and actors to the remote setting in British Columbia, Altman   
had the set built from scratch according to specific historical parameters. Cast and crew lived in the buildings, which gradually emerged as the town of Presbyterian Church that is built up throughout the film. As Janet Walker and Richard Slotkin have argued, “the western is history,” but its representations onscreen often sketch a particular history that focuses on broad themes, rather than lived experience.  
>  
>  
In bringing the cast and crew to the west (and, specifically, the Pacific Northwest), Altman focuses on history lived out in the minute details of daily existence   
in the Pacific Northwest in 1901.

(I think that *McCabe* offers a more nuanced, more holistic view of a town's development on the borderline of the wild west and modernity, but that's just my opinion.) My biggest critique of *Heaven's Gate* would be that, as much as it's marketed and discussed as a subversive, revisionist western, it ends up being a very familiar good vs. evil conflict, with Sam Waterston as a mustache-twirling villain on one side and the most stereotypical virtuous huddled masses of immigrants on the other.

McCabe is great. Altman is a much better overall filmmaker. Nashville is up there with the GOATs imo. 

But 8 out of 10 times, I'm going to watch Heaven's Gate over Mrs. Miller. Telling a good story is just one component of making a film. And I can understand that that is more important to you than spectacle, as it is to a lot of folks. But give me spectacle, almost every time. 

That said - and this is not at all to persuade you - but I really disagree with your POV on the archetypes. They are pretty on-the-nose; but because to Cimino (and to me) it was an on-the-nose time. For example, in the scene you cite - Hupbert, and the peasants, are often more concerned with the high-minded ideals of freedom and independence. So Kristofferson is, quite literally saying 'ideals are fine; but if you're dead they don't matter much'.

This is a leftist film and, as a leftist, I think capitalists - with the backing of the President - fighting a guerrilla war against a bunch of unarmed immigrants...well that's about as black-and-white, and as blunt, as life gets.

I'm absolutely a fan of spectacle as well. One of my all-time favorite films is *Fantasia* (1940, and that -- for a mainstream feature film, anyway -- perhaps cinema's purest example of audiovisual spectacle unencumbered by plot or characterization. And spectacle is what I enjoy most about *Heaven's Gate*. 

I guess we're getting at is that politically engaged filmmaking, by its very nature, has a tendency towards binaries, towards black-and-white splitting. I guess I prefer *McCabe & Mrs. Miller*, a film with quite a few thematic and aesthetic similarities, in part because its morality is messier, more complex, more ambiguous. (To quote Jean Renoir's Octave in *La règle du jeu*, "in this world, there is one awful thing, and that is that everyone has his reasons.") We don't have any nameless crowds virtuous, hardworking, family-oriented immigrants; our titular hero is literally a pimp, and is in some sense as exploitative as his corporate adversaries. 

Another film to bring up in this discussion -- because it's an undeniable influence on both films we're discussing -- is *The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance*, the quintessential Old Hollywood western about a town's growth during the death of the old west and simultaneous birth of modernity.

As you are a fan of the film and are perhaps more familiar with the differences in the various releases, can you please clarify, was the Christopher Walken character significantly altered in the theatrical cut?

I'm reasonably certain that my first viewing of the film was the theatrical cut, and I wasn't that impressed.  I had a complete reversal on that point, both for the film overall as well as Walken's character, when I watched the director's cut.  It was bothering me that I couldn't pinpoint why my first viewing was so negative on his character when I was watching it that second time, so I'm curious if you know if the character was greatly reduced in the first cut.

If I recall, the 'theatrical cut' was actually 4 or 5 manglings. Since the studio was actively failing as the movie was bombing, they tried everything they could to find a cut that would be more successful. 

The cut thats on Amazon was the first real attempt to get back to the director's vision, and then the Criterion is the only available director approved cut. 

All of which is to say, some versions are like an hour shorter. So you could have missed sooo much in that cut.

Yeah, I would agree with you on McCabe's virtues over Heaven's Gate. Altman was certainly a man who understood ambiguity. But I would also say that Altman and Cimino are getting at fundamentally different ideas about the West. 

Deadwood synthesizes both these films in its 3rd season, and in that instance the political ambiguity of the show also disappears in the face of the way immigrant miners were treated. This was a real life horror show, only different from the time's treatment of Native Americans in scale. 

I think the Renoir quote is great, and revealing, but the bounce back from that line of thinking is dangerous, too - how can you judge anyone or anything if you rely too heavily on moral relativism in your guiding ideals?

But, as you say, we are now at the political part of the argument. Luckily, we don't expect art to solve this for us :) The truth is that, personally, I am much more in line with Altman's moral philosophy than Cimino's, while I readily acknowledge that some things are *just evil* and we can call them as such. 

Incidentally, I hate Oppenheimer for this reason, in large part. To me, as a Marxist and a humanist, the A bomb is the most evil thing ever unleashed on this earth, and there should be no ambiguity there when portraying its creator. 

(I'm not asking you to argue Oppenheimer with me, but simply pointing out that - to your point - *my political ideals* sometimes prevent me from enjoying works of art.(
Also, this is a fun convo, you have a lot of context I don't, even though we've seen and thought about a lot of the same films.
Oh you must watch Cleopatra then!
Oh yeah! I haven't seen that in probs 20 years ahahah. Will have to go back, thanks for the reminder!

It is absolutely to Old Hollywood what *Heaven's Gate* is to New Hollywood. (I do think *Heaven's Gate* is in all likelihood the better film.) 

Would highly recommend the making-of documentary as well, which might tell a more dramatic, compelling story than the film itself.
